title: What is dark matter?
subtitle: The invisible cosmos
subject: sciences
description: No one has ever seen it. Yet without it, galaxies would come apart. Dark matter is the invisible glue of the universe.

hero.hook: Picture an invisible glue holding the galaxies together. You cannot see it, but you can see what it holds.

blocks.text: You feel the wind without seeing it: branches move, hair flies. **Dark matter** is a little like that on the scale of the cosmos. It does not shine, it does not reflect light, and it blocks no ray. We only “see” it through what it moves.
It seems to make up about **27%** of the universe, five times more than all the ordinary matter: stars, planets, gas. Without it, galaxies would spin too fast to hold together.

sections.title: Stars moving too fast at the edge

blocks.text: In the **1970s**, the American astronomer **Vera Rubin** measured the speed of stars in spiral galaxies. In the solar system, the farther you are from the Sun, the more slowly you orbit. She expected the same pattern.

blocks.caption: Dark matter gives itself away through its gravitational pull on clusters of galaxies

blocks.text: But the stars at the rim were turning **just as fast** as those near the center. With only the visible mass, they should have flown off. Something invisible had to hold them back: a **halo**, a spherical shell of unseen mass wrapped around the galaxy. The [[galaxy rotation curve]] became the flagship evidence for dark matter.
Vera Rubin had to fight for years to be taken seriously. Princeton kept its astronomy doctorate closed to her because she was a woman, right up to 1975.

sections.title: What is it made from? The search goes on

blocks.text: It is not ordinary matter, the kind called **baryonic**, made of protons and neutrons, because it does not interact with light. It passes through the Earth and through us without leaving a visible trace.

The favorite candidate for a long time was the **WIMP**, a weakly interacting massive particle, something heavy from outside the [[Standard Model]], the theory that describes the known elementary particles. Detectors filled with **liquid xenon**, buried underground, wait for one rare collision. So far there is no clear success. Others bet on the **axion**, an ultra-light particle, or on a theory of gravity that needs rewriting. In the meantime, dark matter bends space and creates [[Gravitational lensing]], which warps the light that passes close to a massive object.

sections.title: And dark energy, the other mystery

blocks.text: Dark matter pulls things together. [[Dark energy]], discovered in **1998**, does the opposite: it speeds up the **expansion of the universe**, the steady drifting apart of the galaxies. They move away faster and faster, when gravity should be slowing them down.

It seems to account for about **68%** of the cosmos. Together with dark matter, that makes **95%** of the universe invisible. Everything we can see, atoms and light, is just **5%**, a thin foam on top.
In the very distant future, dark energy could push the other galaxies so far away that they become invisible from the Milky Way, leaving an almost empty sky.

On one side, the indirect evidence keeps piling up: galactic rotation, the **cosmic microwave background**, the fossil radiation of the young universe, and the filament structure of the universe. On the other, not one direct detection of a particle.

The 21st century will have to decide: a new family of particles, or a new way of thinking about gravity. Dark matter is not a minor detail of the sky. It is the laboratory where tomorrow's physics is being invented.
Dark matter makes up **27%** of the universe. We prove it through its gravity on stars and on light, even though no one has ever seen it directly.
